## 301 vs 308: what's the difference?

Both codes mean "this resource has moved permanently." The difference is what a client may do with the request. After a 301, a client is allowed to turn a POST into a GET, and browsers do. After a 308, the client must send the same method and body to the new URI. Both are cacheable by default, and both are defined today in RFC 9110 (June 2022).

**What each code means.** RFC 9110 gives 301 and 308 the same opening definition. The target resource "has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). For both codes the server SHOULD send a Location header with the preferred new URI, and the user agent MAY use it to redirect automatically. RFC 9110 puts 301, 302, 307 and 308 in the same group: redirects that point to a different URI given in the Location header.

**Method and body.**
- **301:** RFC 9110 lets a user agent change POST to GET "for historical reasons," and says to use 308 if you don't want that. It also explains the history. In HTTP/1.0, 301 and 302 were meant to keep the method. Early browsers disagreed on whether to resend POST as POST or as GET, and "Prevailing practice eventually converged on changing the method to GET." So 307 and 308 were added to mark redirects that keep the method. MDN says that under the Fetch Standard, a browser that gets a 301 in response to a POST does send a GET next (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/301).
- **308:** RFC 7538, which first defined 308, says it is like 301 "except that it does not allow changing the request method from POST to GET" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).
- **The request body:** RFC 9110's general redirect rule says the user agent SHOULD resend the original request with only certain changes. It removes the body-related headers (Content-Type, Content-Length and so on) only when the method has been changed to GET or HEAD. So after a 308, the original body is sent again. After a 301 that turns POST into GET, the body is dropped. MDN's 308 page says the same: "The request method and the body will not be modified" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/308).
- **Wording difference:** RFC 9110's own 308 section doesn't contain a "MUST NOT change the request method" sentence. The 307 section has one, but 308 doesn't. In RFC 9110 the method-keeping rule for 308 comes from the 3xx overview and from RFC 7538.

**Where the sources disagree.** MDN's 308 page says "A 301 Moved Permanently requires the request method and the body to remain unchanged" and that older clients get this wrong by switching to GET. That doesn't match RFC 9110, which explicitly allows POST→GET on a 301, or MDN's own 301 page, which calls the switch to GET "permitted by the HTTP specification." I'd go with RFC 9110: on a 301, changing POST to GET is allowed, not a client bug.

**Caching.** RFC 9110 says both 301 and 308 are "heuristically cacheable." That means a cache may store and reuse them with an estimated lifetime, unless the method definition or explicit cache controls say otherwise. Section 15.1 lists both codes among the heuristically cacheable ones. RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching) explains that this applies to responses that don't state their own freshness. Earlier specs called this "cacheable by default," which is the wording RFC 7538 uses for 308 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html).

**Where they're specified.** The current spec is RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (June 2022): §15.4.2 for 301 and §15.4.9 for 308. RFC 9110 obsoletes RFC 7231, the earlier home of 301, and RFC 7538 (April 2015), the standalone 308 spec. RFC 7538 itself replaced the Experimental RFC 7238. RFC 9110 also notes that 308 is newer (June 2014), so some clients may not recognise it.
